vignette: Tien Nguyen was seventeen when the convoy hit the ridge. One moment he was scanning the dust-choked road ahead; the next, the world collapsed into a cacophony of ripping metal and shouting, followed by the sharp, rhythmic crack of incoming fire. He scrambled over a fallen comrade’s legs, his hands slick with dirt and cordite, screaming orders that no one heard. He remembered gripping the man’s shoulder straps, pulling, but the weight of the body and the relentless snap of rounds overhead left him paralyzed until the dust settled. That afternoon on the ridge became the anchor of his life. Within weeks of returning to his California hometown, Tien found himself unable to relax even when the doors were locked and the windows sealed. He stopped leaving his apartment unless absolutely necessary, and when he did, ordinary sounds—a dropped book, a distant car backfiring—sent him vaulting behind the sofa, heart hammering against his ribs. He took to running through the empty industrial districts at night, jumping curbs and sprinting toward traffic just to feel something manageable, to outrun the quiet that felt more dangerous than the street. His conviction that he belonged nowhere and could never trust anyone pushed him toward that reckless running, as if proving he could still survive the danger he expected around every corner would somehow balance the books. That same isolation made every quiet moment feel like an invitation for the past to return. While developing photographs in his dimly lit back room, the click of his mechanical shutter instantly dragged a memory forward with a terrifying, high-definition clarity. He would see the exact shade of his friend’s uniform, smell the burnt wiring, and feel a white-hot rage build in his chest until his hands shook. His inability to relax kept his nervous system permanently wound, and every time he flinched at a sudden noise, the spike of adrenaline acted like a magnifying glass, making those traumatic memories flash brighter and more insistent. The more his body braced for an attack that never came, the more his mind convinced him that he was fundamentally untrustworthy and alone, cementing his belief that he would always be the one left behind. The rage that flooded his chest whenever he remembered the ridge did not fade when he put the camera down; instead, it hardened into a rigid conviction that he had failed to protect others and that he was broken beyond repair. He tried to shoot street photography to stay grounded, but the sudden flashes from other cameras or the heavy thud of a delivery truck’s doors triggered immediate panic. He would drop his gear and bolt, convinced he was under fire. One afternoon, while waiting for a light rail station, a construction pile driver struck the pavement with a sound like a mortar impact. Tien dropped to his knees, scrambling over bystanders to reach the concrete wall, his breath coming in short, sharp gasps. A group of commuters stepped back, their faces narrowing with suspicion. Tien fled before he could apologize, his chest tight with the certain knowledge that he had nowhere to go and no one who truly understood what he had survived. He stopped taking assignments altogether, leaving his portfolio gathering dust on a shelf, and the gallery that had offered him a debut show never heard from him again. By the time he sat across from a therapist, Tien’s apartment was a fortress of blackout curtains and heavy blankets, though he still could not relax even when the space felt completely secure. He had come to believe that his body was permanently set to a danger setting, and that every ordinary sound was a prelude to catastrophe. The memories still rose unbidden, vivid and furious, reinforcing his guilt and his isolation. He sought help not because he expected a sudden fix, but because the sleepless nights and the reckless running were beginning to cost him his livelihood and his last tether to the world. He was terrified that if he opened his eyes too wide, the ridge would swallow him whole, but he was also desperate for a place where he would finally be allowed to belong.
